tasks.description: Proofread articles — The Church Fathers on the Eucharist

result.name: The Church Fathers on the Eucharist

debates.before: wrote seven letters to churches across Asia Minor
debates.after: wrote seven surviving letters, mostly to churches in Asia Minor, as well as one to the church at Rome and one to Polycarp
debates.concern: The seven authentic letters traditionally attributed to Ignatius were not all addressed to churches in Asia Minor: one was addressed to the church at Rome and one to Polycarp personally.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Revise the description to reflect the destinations of the seven surviving letters.
debates.comment: The revision is more precise and corrects the misattribution of all seven letters to churches in Asia Minor.

debates.before: instructed new converts preparing for baptism in a series of lectures delivered during Holy Week
debates.after: instructed newly baptized Christians in a series of mystagogical lectures delivered during Easter week
debates.concern: Cyril's Mystagogical Catecheses were addressed to the newly baptized after their initiation, not to converts preparing for baptism during Holy Week.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify the audience as newly baptized Christians and place the lectures after baptism during Easter week.
debates.comment: An important liturgical and historical distinction; Cyril's Mystagogical Catecheses were indeed given to the newly baptized during Easter week.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Birth of Christ

debates.section: A Date Anchored in History, If Not Precisely
debates.before: The Church has nonetheless always reckoned its calendar from Dionysius's date, and by the fourth century had fixed December 25 in the West as the liturgical commemoration of the Nativity.
debates.after: The Western Christian calendar eventually adopted Dionysius's dating system, although other Christian traditions have used different calendar eras; by the fourth century, Rome had established December 25 as the liturgical commemoration of the Nativity.
debates.concern: The word "always" is inaccurate: Dionysius's era was adopted gradually and has not been the calendar era used by every Christian tradition. The original wording also compresses the history of the December 25 observance into a claim about the Church as a whole.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the adoption of Dionysius's dating system and specify Rome or the Western Church when describing the fourth-century December 25 observance.
debates.comment: The revision correctly avoids the historical inaccuracy of 'always' regarding Dionysius's system and clarifies the Western origin of December 25.

debates.before: a mission that begins in earnest at Pentecost, thirty-three years later.
debates.after: a mission that begins in earnest at Pentecost, roughly three decades later.
debates.concern: The exact interval between Jesus' birth and Pentecost is uncertain because both the date of the Nativity and the chronology of Jesus' public ministry and death are debated. Presenting Pentecost as exactly thirty-three years later is unnecessarily precise.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the exact interval with an approximate expression, or qualify it as a traditional chronology.
debates.comment: Switching to 'roughly three decades later' avoids false precision on an unresolved chronological point.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Pentecost
Proofread articles — Resurrection & Ascension

debates.before: He appeared to the assembled Eleven in the upper room, twice, a week apart, so that the doubting Thomas could touch His wounds.
debates.after: He appeared to the assembled disciples in the upper room, first without Thomas and then, a week later, with Thomas present so that he could touch Christ's wounds.
debates.concern: According to John 20:19–29, Thomas was absent from the first appearance in the upper room, so the first gathering was not the assembled Eleven. The sentence also incorrectly makes it sound as though the first appearance occurred specifically so Thomas could touch Christ's wounds.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify the first gathering as the disciples assembled without Thomas and the second as the gathering at which Thomas was present.
debates.comment: The revision correctly notes Thomas's absence from the first appearance, preventing a contradiction of John 20.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Our Lady of the Pillar

debates.before: Traditional — papal approbation; feast of Our Lady of the Pillar, 12 October
debates.after: Traditional — liturgical recognition; feast of Our Lady of the Pillar, 12 October
debates.concern: The article explicitly says that this apostolic-era apparition is not formally approved in the modern canonical sense. Calling its status “papal approbation” is therefore misleading and may suggest a formal approval that the article denies. The fact should describe the tradition's liturgical recognition without implying a modern canonical approval.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace “papal approbation” with wording describing the shrine's liturgical recognition or established devotion, unless a specific papal act of approbation is documented.
debates.comment: Accurate correction to avoid contradicting the article's own stance on canonical approval.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Council of Jerusalem

debates.before: Why, then, are you now putting God to the test by placing on the shoulders of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?
debates.after: Why, then, are you now putting God to the test by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we have been able to bear?
debates.concern: The wording attributed to the NABRE does not match the NABRE text of Acts 15:10, which uses "on the neck," "our ancestors," and "we." The quoted wording appears to combine or paraphrase wording from another translation while identifying it as NABRE.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the quotation with the exact NABRE wording, or identify the quotation as coming from the translation whose wording is actually used.
debates.comment: Accurate correction to the specific translation text.

debates.before: It hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.
debates.after: For it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us.
debates.concern: The Douay-Rheims text of Acts 15:28 includes the opening word "For." Presenting the shortened wording as a complete quotation without an omission marker misidentifies the translation's exact text.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Restore the omitted opening word or use an ellipsis to indicate that the quotation has been abridged.
debates.comment: Restores the exact word used in the Douay-Rheims translation.

debates.before: James, presiding as head of the Jerusalem church, then proposed the council's judgment.
debates.after: James, a leading figure in the Jerusalem church, then proposed the council's judgment.
debates.concern: Acts 15 records Peter's speech, followed by James's proposal, but it does not explicitly say that James presided over the gathering. Calling him the presiding head may overstate what the text establishes and may imply a formal role that is disputed in historical interpretation.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use wording that reflects James's prominent role without asserting that he presided unless a specific historical source supports that claim.
debates.comment: Avoids an interpretive overstatement regarding James's formal role.

debates.before: It asked of them only a small number of practical requirements meant to preserve fellowship at table between Jewish and Gentile believers.
debates.after: It asked of them only a small number of requirements intended to govern fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers, including at table.
debates.concern: Describing all four requirements as merely practical table-fellowship rules is an interpretive simplification. The prohibitions concerning sexual immorality and blood have broader religious and moral significance, and the precise rationale of the decree is debated.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the explanation of the requirements rather than reducing them exclusively to table fellowship.
debates.comment: Provides a more precise theological characterization of the decree's requirements.

debates.before: The Council of Jerusalem established, in the Church's own founding generation, the pattern that would govern every ecumenical council afterward.
debates.after: The Council of Jerusalem is often regarded as an early model for later councils, although it is not an ecumenical council in the later technical sense.
debates.concern: The original wording makes a broad historical and ecclesiological claim that the Jerusalem gathering established the governing pattern for every later ecumenical council. The event is commonly treated as a precedent or prototype, but its relationship to later ecumenical councils should not be stated as an unqualified institutional continuity.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Present the Jerusalem gathering as an important precedent or model, while distinguishing it from the later category of ecumenical councils.
debates.comment: Adds necessary historical nuance regarding the nature of ecumenical councils.

debates.before: Paul would later defend this decision at length in his Letter to the Galatians.
debates.after: In his Letter to the Galatians, Paul would later defend the freedom of Gentile believers from circumcision and reliance on the Mosaic Law.
debates.concern: Galatians strongly defends Gentile freedom from circumcision and the Mosaic Law, but it does not explicitly recount or defend the Jerusalem decree as such. The wording therefore presents a debated relationship between Galatians and Acts 15 as though it were certain.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Describe Paul's argument in Galatians directly, and avoid saying that he defended the specific decree unless the chronology and identification are qualified.
debates.comment: Clarifies the specific connection between the letter and Paul's theological arguments.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Persecution under Nero

debates.before: Tradition holds that both St. Peter and St. Paul were martyred in Rome during this persecution
debates.after: Christian tradition holds that St. Peter and St. Paul were martyred in Rome during Nero's reign
debates.concern: The deaths of Peter and Paul in Rome are strongly rooted in early Christian tradition, but directly connecting both martyrdoms to the specific persecution following the fire is less certain. The present wording can make that connection sound historically established.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Separate the traditional Roman martyrdoms from the more specific and uncertain claim that both occurred during the fire-related persecution.
debates.comment: A meaningful historical correction that properly separates the martyrdoms from the specific fire-related persecution.

debates.before: It was the see that Peter and Paul had both led and died for
debates.after: It was the see traditionally associated with Peter's leadership and with the martyrdom of Peter and Paul
debates.concern: Paul is not generally understood to have led the Roman see or served as its bishop. The sentence incorrectly implies that both apostles held the Roman episcopate, even though Paul ministered in Rome and was martyred there.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Distinguish Paul's ministry and martyrdom in Rome from Peter's traditional leadership of the Roman church.
debates.comment: Corrects a genuine theological/historical error by removing the implication that Paul was a leader of the Roman see.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Destruction of the Temple

debates.before: the daily sacrifices that had defined Jewish worship since the time of Solomon's Temple came to an end
debates.after: the daily sacrifices that had been offered in the Second Temple came to an end
debates.concern: The wording implies an uninterrupted sacrificial system since Solomon's Temple, overlooking the destruction of the First Temple, the Babylonian exile, and the rebuilding of the Temple. The sacrifices ended in AD 70 specifically with the destruction of the Second Temple.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Limit the claim to the sacrificial worship of the Second Temple.
debates.comment: An important theological and historical correction regarding the continuity of the Temple sacrifices.

debates.before: marked the effective end of Second Temple Judaism
debates.after: marked the end of the Second Temple period and transformed Jewish religious life
debates.concern: The phrase can misleadingly suggest that Judaism itself effectively ended in AD 70. The destruction ended the Second Temple period and Temple-centered sacrificial worship, while Jewish communal and religious life continued and developed in multiple directions.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Describe the end of the Second Temple period and the transformation of Judaism rather than an effective end to Second Temple Judaism without qualification.
debates.comment: Provides a more precise historical framing that avoids any implication that Judaism itself ended.

debates.before: See ye all these things? Amen I say to you, there shall not be left here a stone upon a stone.
debates.after: See ye all these things? Amen I say to you, there shall not be left here a stone upon a stone, that shall not be destroyed.
debates.concern: The quotation is presented as Matthew 24:2 in the Douay-Rheims translation but omits the verse's concluding clause, "that shall not be destroyed." As quoted, it is incomplete while being presented as a complete quotation.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Restore the omitted clause or use an ellipsis to indicate that the quotation has been shortened.
debates.comment: Restores the complete biblical verse for accuracy in a direct quotation.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Persecution under Domitian

debates.section: Suspicion at the Heart of the Court
debates.before: The Roman historian Tertullian
debates.after: The Christian writer Tertullian
debates.concern: Tertullian was a Christian theologian and ecclesiastical writer, not a Roman historian. The description misidentifies his role and could cause readers to misunderstand the nature of his testimony.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the description with an accurate characterization of Tertullian.
debates.comment: Tertullian is well-known as a Christian apologist and theologian rather than a Roman historian.

debates.section: Suspicion at the Heart of the Court
debates.before: that cruelty had turned decisively against the Christians of the empire
debates.after: later Christian writers associated his reign with hostility toward some Christians and other groups
debates.concern: The article presents a broad, systematic Domitianic persecution of Christians as established history. The surviving evidence is limited and disputed: ancient sources document proceedings against particular individuals, but do not clearly establish an empire-wide persecution comparable to Nero's.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the scope of the alleged persecution throughout the article and distinguish documented cases from later Christian memory.
debates.comment: The nature and scale of Domitianic persecution are genuinely debated; softening the claim improves accuracy.

debates.before: Both were condemned, according to the ancient historian Dio Cassius, on charges of "atheism," the standard Roman accusation against those who abandoned the state religion for what officials regarded as a strange and dangerous foreign superstition.
debates.after: Dio Cassius reports that Flavius Clemens was condemned for "atheism"; later Christian tradition associated this charge, and the broader persecution, with other figures including Manius Acilius Glabrio.
debates.concern: The sentence attributes the same charge and evidentiary basis to both men while also describing "atheism" as a standard accusation against Christians. The ancient evidence and the precise relationship between Glabrio's prosecution, Christianity, and a Domitianic persecution are more limited and should not be stated so categorically.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Separate what Dio explicitly reports about Clemens from later or less certain claims about Glabrio, and qualify the interpretation of the charge.
debates.comment: Nuancing Dio Cassius's report avoids overstating the historical consensus regarding Glabrio's Christianity.

debates.before: John was banished, in his own words, "on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus."
debates.after: John said that he was on Patmos "on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus"; later tradition understood this as an exile or banishment.
debates.concern: Revelation 1:9 states that John was on Patmos for this reason, but it does not explicitly say that he was banished. Presenting banishment as John's own wording overstates what the cited verse says.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Distinguish the biblical statement from the later interpretation that John had been exiled there.
debates.comment: Revelation 1:9 mentions Patmos and the word of God, but tradition is required to explicitly connect it to banishment.

debates.before: during Domitian's reign's final year
debates.after: during the later years traditionally associated with Domitian's reign
debates.concern: The exact final year of Domitian's reign is not established by the cited tradition. Revelation is commonly dated to Domitian's reign, but the specific year of John's exile is uncertain.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the unsupported precision unless a reliable source specifically establishes the date.
debates.comment: Dating the exile to the exact final year is overly specific given scholarly uncertainty.

debates.before: Domitian's persecution ended as abruptly as it had begun:
debates.after: The reported hostility associated with Domitian's reign ended abruptly:
debates.concern: The wording treats a clearly defined, empire-wide persecution as an established event, although the evidence more securely documents individual prosecutions and later traditions about a broader persecution.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use more cautious language unless the article supplies evidence for a formal or empire-wide persecution.
debates.comment: Reflecting the traditional nature of the hostility avoids asserting a fully proven systemic persecution.

debates.before: Flavius Clemens; Manius Acilius Glabrio; exile of St. John to Patmos
debates.after: Flavius Clemens; Manius Acilius Glabrio; traditional association of St. John with exile on Patmos
debates.concern: The fact line presents John's exile as certain, although the biblical text says only that John was on Patmos and the interpretation that this was a Domitianic banishment comes from tradition. It also places all three cases under the same implied category of established martyrs or victims.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify John's exile as traditional and clarify the status of the individual cases.
debates.comment: Distinguishing between historical figures and the traditional association of St. John improves precision in the quick facts.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Ignatius of Antioch
Proofread articles — Trajan's Rescript

debates.before: a test Pliny understood no genuine Christian could be compelled to perform
debates.after: a test that he used to determine whether those accused would renounce their Christian profession
debates.concern: Pliny's account shows that some accused Christians did perform the required sacrifice and were released; it does not say that a genuine Christian could not be compelled to perform it. The wording also turns a Roman administrative test into a theological judgment about who was a 'genuine' Christian.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Describe the sacrifice as Pliny's test for persistence in the Christian confession, without attributing to him a judgment about what a genuine Christian could or could not do.
debates.comment: An important factual and theological correction regarding how Pliny's test functioned in practice.

debates.before: set a pattern of official policy that would govern the treatment of Christians across the empire for decades to come
debates.after: provided an influential precedent for the treatment of Christians in some provincial cases
debates.concern: Trajan's rescript answered Pliny's specific administrative question; it was not a comprehensive empire-wide statute or uniformly governing policy. Enforcement varied by governor and locality, and the rescript itself did not establish a universal legal framework for decades.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Present the rescript as a significant precedent or policy statement whose influence was substantial but whose application was not uniform across the empire.
debates.comment: Corrects a common misconception about Trajan's rescript operating as a universal statute across the whole empire.

debates.before: the law still required their punishment
debates.after: those who were formally denounced and persisted in the Christian confession were to be punished under the practice Trajan approved
debates.concern: The rescript does not clearly identify a general law that required punishment simply for being Christian. It instructs Pliny how to handle accused persons in this case, while also forbidding officials from seeking Christians out and rejecting anonymous accusations.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Avoid describing the rescript as enforcing a general statutory requirement unless the specific legal basis is identified.
debates.comment: More accurately reflects the specific nuances of Trajan's instructions against active hunting and anonymous tips.

debates.section: The First Roman Account of Christian Worship
debates.before: it stands as the earliest surviving non-Christian eyewitness account of Christian worship and moral practice
debates.after: it stands as one of the earliest surviving non-Christian accounts describing Christian worship and moral practice
debates.concern: Calling it the earliest surviving non-Christian eyewitness account is too absolute and potentially misleading. Pliny conducted an investigation and reports testimony, but the letter is not normally treated as a firsthand eyewitness description of a Christian worship gathering; earlier non-Christian testimony about Christians also survives in Tacitus.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Describe the letter more narrowly as one of the earliest surviving non-Christian descriptions of Christian worship and communal practice.
debates.comment: Corrects an overstatement, given that Pliny was reporting testimony and investigation rather than directly observing a service himself.

debates.section: The First Roman Account of Christian Worship
debates.before: confirming from an entirely hostile, official vantage point exactly the kind of ordinary, disciplined community life the Christians themselves already understood their gatherings to embody
debates.after: describing, from an official Roman perspective, a community whose reported practices included worship and ethical commitments
debates.concern: The source does not establish that Pliny was 'entirely hostile,' nor does it confirm that his description exactly matched how Christians understood their own communal life. Those are interpretive claims that go beyond the evidence of the letter.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Separate what Pliny reports from the article's interpretation of Christian self-understanding, and avoid claiming exact confirmation.
debates.comment: Removes loaded interpretive language ('entirely hostile') that goes beyond the text of the letter.

debates.before: For nearly two centuries afterward, this same uneasy, provisional policy would leave every Christian in the empire living, in effect, one denunciation away from martyrdom.
debates.after: For much of the second and early third centuries, the rescript remained an important reference point, although the practical danger to Christians varied greatly by region, governor, and period.
debates.concern: The sentence turns a locally addressed and inconsistently applied policy into a uniform condition affecting every Christian in the empire. It also presents martyrdom as the predictable result of any denunciation, whereas accusations could be dismissed, withdrawn, or resolved without execution.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify both the duration and the empire-wide scope, and avoid the sweeping claim that every Christian was continuously one denunciation away from martyrdom.
debates.comment: Significantly improves historical precision by avoiding the over-generalized claim that every Christian lived one denunciation away from martyrdom.

debates.before: Later Christian apologists, writing decades afterward, would return again and again to Pliny's own grudging admission of Christian innocence as evidence
debates.after: Later Christian writers could point to Pliny's report that his investigation had found no crimes corresponding to the accusations as evidence
debates.concern: The article does not identify the alleged Christian apologists or demonstrate that they repeatedly used Pliny's letter in this way. The phrase 'grudging admission of Christian innocence' also overstates Pliny's conclusion: he reported their communal practices and lack of ordinary crimes, but did not declare Christian innocence in general.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Name specific later writers if this claim is retained, and describe Pliny's evidence more precisely as a report about the practices and conduct he investigated.
debates.comment: Removes the unsupported reference to Christian apologists repeatedly citing Pliny, replacing it with a more grounded statement.

debates.before: Nearly two hundred years would pass before an emperor finally granted the Church anything more than this same uneasy, provisional tolerance Trajan first sketched out
debates.after: Roughly two centuries later, imperial measures under Gallienus and, more decisively, the edicts of Galerius and Constantine provided Christians with forms of toleration and legal recognition beyond Trajan's rescript
debates.concern: The statement is too absolute and obscures important developments before the fourth century, including Gallienus's policy toward Christians around 260. It also conflates toleration, restoration of confiscated property, and legal recognition, which occurred at different times and under different emperors.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify the relevant later measures and distinguish temporary toleration from the broader legal settlement associated with the early fourth century.
debates.comment: Correctly notes earlier imperial measures like Gallienus's tolerance rather than painting the two-century gap as absolute.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Polycarp

debates.before: While in Rome Polycarp also won back many who had been led astray by heretics.
debates.after: While in Rome Polycarp encountered Marcion, whom he rejected as a heretic.
debates.concern: The surviving account, reported by Irenaeus, says that Polycarp encountered Marcion and denounced him; it does not establish that Polycarp won back many people from heresy. The present wording appears to turn an isolated encounter into an unsupported mass conversion.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the claim with the specific, documented account or qualify it as uncertain.
debates.comment: The revision aligns the text specifically with the Irenaeus account regarding Marcion.

debates.before: he was urged to save his life by cursing Christ.
debates.after: he was urged to save his life by swearing by Caesar and reviling Christ.
debates.concern: The Martyrdom of Polycarp describes the proconsul's demand that Polycarp swear by Caesar and revile Christ. Reducing this to an instruction to curse Christ omits the central legal and political element of the trial and is not an accurate representation of the account.
debates.suggestedCorrection: State the proconsul's demand more precisely.
debates.comment: Adding the demand to swear by Caesar accurately reflects the Roman trial context.

debates.before: c. 155, Smyrna (burned at the stake)
debates.after: c. 155, Smyrna (executed by fire and sword)
debates.concern: The article itself says that the flames did not consume Polycarp and that he was ultimately killed with a dagger. 'Burned at the stake' can therefore misleadingly suggest that burning was the direct cause of death.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use wording that reflects both the attempted burning and the subsequent stabbing, or state simply that he was martyred at Smyrna.
debates.comment: More accurately reflects the text's own account of the dagger being the direct cause of death.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Justin Martyr
Proofread articles — Martyrs of Lyons

debates.before: Both traced their spiritual lineage back to St. Polycarp of Smyrna, himself a disciple of the Apostle John
debates.after: Irenaeus traced his spiritual lineage back to St. Polycarp of Smyrna, himself a disciple of the Apostle John
debates.concern: Irenaeus explicitly identified himself as a hearer of Polycarp, but the surviving account does not securely establish that Pothinus also had a direct connection to Polycarp. The sentence presents that connection as certain.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Limit the direct Polycarp connection to Irenaeus unless an authoritative source confirms it for Pothinus.
debates.comment: The revision avoids overstating the direct connection for Pothinus, which is historically uncertain.

debates.before: Gaul itself had received the Gospel only a generation or two earlier, carried across from Asia Minor by missionaries in the circle of St. Polycarp
debates.after: The Christian communities of Gaul had received the Gospel through earlier missionary activity, including connections with Christians from Asia Minor
debates.concern: The precise claim about when Gaul received the Gospel and its transmission specifically by missionaries in Polycarp's circle is more specific than the evidence safely supports. It should be qualified unless documented by a reliable historical source.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use more cautious wording or provide a source for the chronology and the alleged missionary connection.
debates.comment: The original makes overly specific claims about the exact origins of Christianity in Gaul that are not securely documented.

debates.before: The ancient account tells us that even her exhausted torturers confessed themselves outdone by a girl they had expected to break within the hour.
debates.after: The ancient account says that her torturers admitted they could do no more to make her renounce her faith.
debates.concern: The source account describes the torturers' inability to break Blandina, but the expectation that she would break 'within the hour' is an invented or unsupported detail. It presents a dramatic motive and time estimate as historical fact.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the unsupported time estimate and retain only what the ancient account actually reports.
debates.comment: Removing the dramatic, unverified detail about breaking within the hour improves historical accuracy.

debates.section: A Final Martyrdom in the Arena
debates.before: Witnesses recorded that she endured with such visible serenity that the crowd remarked they had never seen a woman suffer so long and so completely without breaking.
debates.after: The account portrays her as enduring the ordeal without renouncing her faith.
debates.concern: The surviving account describes Blandina's endurance, but this sentence attributes a specific remark to the crowd and claims that witnesses recorded it without providing a basis. The wording appears to embellish the source.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the alleged crowd remark unless it can be documented in the source; describe her endurance more cautiously.
debates.comment: The original includes embellishments regarding specific crowd reactions not present in the surviving source text.

debates.before: Every persecuted Christian community has clung to it since
debates.after: Persecuted Christian communities have often found encouragement in it
debates.concern: The universal claim that every persecuted Christian community has clung to this account is sweeping and unsupported. It also turns a devotional interpretation into an asserted historical fact.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the universal claim with qualified language about the account's enduring significance.
debates.comment: The original's absolute claim is hyperbole; the revision offers a more sober and defensible historical tone.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — St. Irenaeus

debates.before: though himself firmly of the Roman practice
debates.after: though himself committed to preserving communion amid differing practices
debates.concern: Irenaeus's own background was associated with the Asian date for Easter, and the surviving account presents him as urging Pope Victor not to break communion over the dispute. Describing him as firmly of the Roman practice is therefore misleading and appears historically incorrect.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the claim that Irenaeus followed the Roman practice, and describe instead his effort to preserve communion despite differing Easter customs.
debates.comment: Irenaeus is historically noted for urging Victor to maintain communion despite calendar differences rather than strictly adhering to the Roman practice.

debates.before: with extraordinary care, book by book, it lays out exactly which bishops in which cities had succeeded one another from the Apostles' own day
debates.after: with extraordinary care, it appeals to the apostolic succession preserved in the Churches, giving particular attention to the succession of bishops at Rome
debates.concern: Against Heresies appeals to succession lists, especially the Roman succession, but the wording suggests that the work provides complete, exact succession lists for bishops in multiple cities extending directly from the Apostles. That is broader and more precise than the surviving evidence supports.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the statement and identify the Roman succession, or other specific succession list, rather than claiming an exact catalogue for the Churches generally.
debates.comment: The revision avoids overstating the completeness of the surviving lists while capturing Irenaeus's actual argument regarding apostolic succession.

debates.text: The eucharistic liturgy that still bears his name continues to be prayed in Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches on the great feasts of the liturgical year
debates.concern: The Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil is celebrated on a specific limited set of days, traditionally including Sundays of Great Lent, Christmas, Epiphany, Holy Thursday, Holy Saturday, and the saint's feast, rather than generally on 'the great feasts.' The wording may therefore overstate or inaccurately characterize its current liturgical use.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the broad reference to the great feasts with a more precise description of the days on which the Byzantine churches celebrate the Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil.

debates.after: continues to be celebrated in Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches on certain major liturgical days, including Christmas, Epiphany, several Sundays of Great Lent, Holy Thursday, and Holy Saturday
debates.comment: The revision provides much greater liturgical precision regarding when the Liturgy of Saint Basil is actually celebrated.

debates.before: In Barcelona he co-founded, with St. Peter Nolasco, the Mercedarian Order, dedicated specifically to ransoming Christian captives held by Muslim powers.
debates.after: In Barcelona, Raymond was associated by tradition with St. Peter Nolasco in the founding of the Mercedarian Order, which was dedicated to ransoming Christian captives held by Muslim powers.
debates.concern: Raymond's role in founding the Mercedarian Order is traditionally reported but is not an uncomplicated established historical fact. The sentence presents the co-founding as certain.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify Raymond's role as traditional or disputed, and verify the precise historical account of the order's foundation.
debates.comment: The revision correctly nuances Raymond's disputed role in founding the Mercedarian Order.

debates.before: It was at his personal request that his younger confrere, St. Thomas Aquinas, composed the Summa Contra Gentiles, intended to aid missionary efforts among Spain's Muslim population.
debates.after: According to a traditional account, Raymond encouraged St. Thomas Aquinas to compose the Summa contra Gentiles, which has sometimes been associated with missionary efforts among Muslims and Jews.
debates.concern: Raymond's personal commissioning of the work and its specific intended audience are debated. The existing wording states both claims too definitively and narrows the work's purpose to Spain's Muslim population.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the attribution to Raymond and avoid presenting the specific missionary purpose as settled fact unless supported by an authoritative source.
debates.comment: The original overstates both the commission and the specific audience, which are debated among scholars.

debates.before: He remains honored today as the patron saint of canon lawyers, a scholar whose careful, systematic work gave the medieval Church its first truly organized body of law.
debates.after: He remains honored today as the patron saint of canon lawyers, a scholar whose careful, systematic work helped organize the medieval Church's developing body of canon law.
debates.concern: Raymond's work on Gregory IX's Decretals was highly influential, but it did not give the Church its first organized body of law. Earlier collections, especially Gratian's Decretum, had already organized substantial bodies of canon law. The phrase 'first truly organized body of law' is materially misleading.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Remove the claim of priority and describe Raymond's contribution as organizing and systematizing an already developing canonical tradition.
debates.comment: The original's claim that this was the 'first truly organized body of law' is materially incorrect given Gratian's earlier work.
